issues.legal_issue: A resolution under Article 252(1) of the Constitution is passed by the House or Houses of a State Legislature, without participation or assent by the Governor.
material_facts: The Houses of the State Legislature passed resolutions authorizing Parliament to legislate on ceilings on urban immovable property and related matters.
The Governor did not participate in passing those resolutions.
The High Court held the legislation inapplicable to the State because the Governor had not participated in the authorization.
issues.conclusion: The resolutions validly authorized Parliament to legislate; the Governor’s participation or assent was not required.
issues.legal_principle: Article 252(1), read in context, uses “Legislatures” to mean the House or Houses of the State Legislature, excluding the Governor. A resolution is distinct from an Act of the legislature, and the Constitution does not require the Governor’s assent to such a resolution. The Court relied on State of Bihar v. Maharajadhiraja Sir Kameshwar Singh of Darbhanga and Ors. [1952] S.C.R. 889 and the reasoning in Jatin Chakravorty v. Sri Justice H. K. Bose; it also treated ratification under Article 368(2) as analogous.

predicates.challenge_to_central_law: A party challenged whether a central law could validly apply to a state.
predicates.multiple_state_houses_passed_authorizing: The Houses of at least two State Legislatures passed resolutions authorizing Parliament to regulate a subject for those states.

issues.definition: When a central law is challenged and the Houses of at least two State Legislatures passed authorizing resolutions, the authorization is effective without the head of state’s assent.

issues.legal_issue: A parliamentary law may regulate only part of a subject that State Legislatures authorized Parliament to regulate under Article 252(1).
material_facts: The State resolutions authorized Parliament to regulate ceilings on urban immovable property and matters connected or ancillary to that subject.
The Act imposed a ceiling on vacant land in urban agglomerations rather than imposing a ceiling based on the monetary value of all immovable property.
The resolutions were passed after State governments had considered proposals concerning urban immovable property, including urban areas and their peripheral areas.
issues.conclusion: Parliament was competent to enact a law imposing a ceiling on vacant urban land, even though the law did not cover every kind of immovable property or use the monetary-value approach urged by the challengers.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 252(1), resolutions on a State subject empower Parliament to legislate on the authorized subject. The resolutions are not hedged with conditions, and Parliament need not exhaust the whole field of that subject in a single law. Entry 18 of List II includes land and buildings, including vacant land. The scope of a State’s surrender of legislative power depends on the language of its resolution, as recognized in R.M.D.C. (Mysore) Private Ltd. v. The State of Mysore.

predicates.challenge_to_central_law: A party challenged Parliament’s competence to enact a law on a subject ordinarily within State legislative authority.
predicates.state_resolutions_authorized_a_subject: State Legislatures passed resolutions authorizing Parliament to regulate a stated subject.
predicates.central_law_regulates_part_of_that_subje: The central law regulates a part, rather than the entirety, of the subject covered by the State resolutions.

issues.definition: If a central law is challenged, State Legislatures authorized Parliament to regulate a subject, and the law regulates part of that subject, Parliament may legislate on that part.

issues.legal_issue: A ceiling law can apply to a covered urban agglomeration even if there is no master plan or the plan does not designate land for compulsory acquisition.
material_facts: The relevant urban agglomeration was specified in the Act’s Schedule.
A master plan had been prepared and later revised and sanctioned for the town.
The challenge asserted that the master plan did not satisfy a local-law requirement to designate land for compulsory acquisition.
The plan contained development proposals, and the municipality had power to acquire land needed to implement such proposals.
issues.conclusion: The alleged deficiency did not prevent the Act from applying to the urban agglomeration. The Act’s application did not depend on the existence of a master plan; where there is no plan, or it does not refer to land as urban land, the Act applies to qualifying land within the local limits of the relevant municipality or other local authority.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2(h), 2(o), 2(n), 3 and 4 of the Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Act define the relevant land, agglomerations and ceiling regime. Section 2(o) provides for urban land both where a master plan identifies it and where there is no plan or the plan does not do so. The word “shall” in Section 244(1)(c) of the Andhra Pradesh (Telengana Area) District Municipalities Act, 1956 is directory in context; a plan is not invalid merely because it omits a proposal designating land for compulsory acquisition. The municipality’s acquisition power under Section 250 supports implementation of a scheme without such designation in the plan. No earlier case is relied on for this issue.

predicates.challenge_to_urban_ceiling_law: A party challenged the application of a ceiling law to an urban agglomeration.
predicates.urban_agglomeration_covered_by_law: The urban agglomeration falls within the areas covered by the law.
predicates.applicability_challenged_for_master_plan: The challenge asserts that the master plan is absent or deficient, including because it omits designation of land for compulsory acquisition.

issues.definition: When a covered urban agglomeration is subject to a challenge based on a master-plan defect, the ceiling law still applies to covered urban land.

issues.legal_issue: A law enacted under Article 252(1) may identify non-sponsoring states and their urban areas for later adoption, and becomes applicable to such a state when its Legislature adopts the law.
material_facts: The Act was enacted after resolutions under Article 252(1) had been passed by multiple states, but Rajasthan had not been among those states.
The Act’s Schedule identified Rajasthan and specified urban agglomerations and categories within it.
A Proclamation of Emergency was in force when the Act was enacted, but the Act’s preamble and Statement of Objects and Reasons showed that Parliament proceeded under Article 252(1), not Article 250.
Rajasthan later passed a resolution adopting the Act under Article 252(1).
issues.conclusion: The Schedule’s identification and categorization of Rajasthan’s urban agglomerations was within Parliament’s competence and was not invalid because Rajasthan had not initially sponsored the Act. The Act applied to Rajasthan from the date of its adoption.
issues.legal_principle: Article 252(1) empowers Parliament, upon resolutions by two or more State Legislatures, to enact a law that applies to the sponsoring states and is capable of adoption by other states; Article 252(2) governs amendment or repeal. Parliament has plenary power over the authorized subject and may structure a uniform law to facilitate later adoption. A law enacted under Article 250 is subject to the limited duration stated in Article 250(2), and adoption under Article 252 concerns a law made under Article 252(1). The Act’s preamble and Statement of Objects and Reasons established that it was enacted under Article 252(1), not Article 250. No earlier case is relied on for this issue.

predicates.challenge_to_legislative_competence: A party challenged Parliament’s competence to apply a law to a state that did not initially authorize it.
predicates.law_enacted_under_multi_state_authorizat: Parliament enacted the law after multiple State Legislatures passed resolutions authorizing legislation on the subject.
predicates.non_sponsoring_state_identified_in_sched: The law identified a state that had not initially passed an authorizing resolution, along with areas within that state.
predicates.state_later_adopted_law: The Legislature of the non-sponsoring state later passed a resolution adopting the law.

issues.definition: If a law made after multi-state authorization identifies a non-sponsoring state and that state later adopts it, the identification is valid and the law applies there after adoption.
